subject: chemistry
pattern: Carries about 7-9 marks in the Karnataka 2nd PUC board paper: a 1-mark (Hoffmann bromamide, carbylamine reaction, Hinsberg reagent), two 2-mark reasoning or named-reaction questions (basic strength of aniline, Gabriel synthesis), a 3-mark question on basic strength order or distinguishing 1°, 2°, 3° amines or diazonium reactions, and sometimes a 5-mark question on preparation of amines or reactions of diazonium salts. Examiners expect balanced equations with reagents and the reason in terms of +I effect, resonance and solvation.

questions.q: What is Hoffmann bromamide degradation reaction? Give the equation.
questions.answer: When an amide is treated with bromine and aqueous or alcoholic NaOH (or KOH), it is converted into a primary amine having one carbon atom less than the amide. RCONH$_2$ + Br$_2$ + 4NaOH → RNH$_2$ + Na$_2$CO$_3$ + 2NaBr + 2H$_2$O. Example: CH$_3$CONH$_2$ gives CH$_3$NH$_2$.

questions.q: What is carbylamine reaction? Give the equation. What is its use?
questions.answer: Aliphatic or aromatic primary amines on heating with chloroform and alcoholic KOH form isocyanides (carbylamines), which have a foul smell. R-NH$_2$ + CHCl$_3$ + 3KOH → R-NC + 3KCl + 3H$_2$O. It is used as a test for primary amines; secondary and tertiary amines do not respond.

questions.q: What is Hinsberg's reagent? What is its use?
questions.answer: Benzenesulphonyl chloride (C$_6$H$_5$SO$_2$Cl) is called Hinsberg's reagent. It is used to distinguish and separate primary, secondary and tertiary amines.

questions.q: Aniline is a weaker base than methylamine (or ammonia). Give reason.
questions.answer: In aniline the lone pair on nitrogen is delocalised into the benzene ring through resonance, so it is less available for protonation. Also, the anilinium ion formed on accepting a proton has fewer resonance structures than aniline, so it is less stable. In methylamine, the +I effect of the CH$_3$ group increases electron density on nitrogen, making the lone pair more available. Hence aniline (pKb 9.38) is much weaker base than methylamine (pKb 3.38) and ammonia (4.75).

questions.q: What is Gabriel phthalimide synthesis? Why can it not be used to prepare aromatic primary amines?
questions.answer: Phthalimide is treated with ethanolic KOH to form potassium phthalimide, which on heating with an alkyl halide gives N-alkylphthalimide; alkaline hydrolysis gives pure primary amine (aliphatic) and sodium phthalate. Phthalimide → (KOH) potassium phthalimide → (R-X) N-alkylphthalimide → (NaOH/H$_2$O) R-NH$_2$ + phthalate. Aromatic primary amines cannot be prepared because aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution with the phthalimide anion (C-X bond in aryl halide is strong due to partial double bond character).

questions.q: Aniline does not undergo Friedel-Crafts reaction. Why?
questions.answer: Friedel-Crafts reaction uses anhydrous AlCl$_3$ as catalyst, which is a Lewis acid. Aniline is a Lewis base because of the lone pair on nitrogen, so it combines with AlCl$_3$ to form a salt (adduct). Nitrogen in this adduct acquires a positive charge and becomes a strongly deactivating group for the ring, so the electrophilic substitution does not take place.

questions.q: Boiling points of primary amines are higher than tertiary amines but lower than alcohols of comparable molecular mass. Explain.
questions.answer: Primary and secondary amines have N-H bonds and form intermolecular hydrogen bonds; tertiary amines have no N-H bond, so they do not associate and have the lowest boiling point. Primary amines have two N-H bonds and therefore more extensive hydrogen bonding than secondary amines. Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, so the N-H...N hydrogen bonds are weaker than O-H...O bonds in alcohols; hence amines boil lower than alcohols. Order: alcohol > primary amine > secondary amine > tertiary amine.

questions.q: How will you distinguish primary, secondary and tertiary amines using benzenesulphonyl chloride (Hinsberg test)?
questions.answer: Primary amine: reacts with benzenesulphonyl chloride to form N-alkylbenzenesulphonamide, which has an acidic hydrogen on nitrogen and therefore dissolves in aqueous KOH. RNH$_2$ + C$_6$H$_5$SO$_2$Cl → C$_6$H$_5$SO$_2$NHR (soluble in alkali). Secondary amine: gives N,N-dialkylbenzenesulphonamide, C$_6$H$_5$SO$_2$NR$_2$, which has no acidic hydrogen and is insoluble in alkali. Tertiary amine: does not react with benzenesulphonyl chloride under these conditions.

questions.q: Arrange the following in the decreasing order of basic strength in aqueous solution and give reason: (C$_2$H$_5$)$_2$NH, (C$_2$H$_5$)$_3$N, C$_2$H$_5$NH$_2$, NH$_3$.
questions.answer: Order: (C$_2$H$_5$)$_2$NH > (C$_2$H$_5$)$_3$N > C$_2$H$_5$NH$_2$ > NH$_3$. Reason: basic strength depends on the +I effect of alkyl groups (increases electron density on N), the steric hindrance to protonation, and the extent of solvation (hydrogen bonding with water) of the ammonium ion formed. Alkyl groups increase electron density, so all ethylamines are stronger than NH$_3$. In the tertiary amine, the ammonium ion has only one N-H bond for hydrogen bonding with water and the bulky groups hinder protonation, so solvation is least and the tertiary amine is weaker than the secondary amine. The secondary amine has the best balance of +I effect and solvation.

questions.q: Explain Sandmeyer reaction and Gattermann reaction of benzenediazonium chloride with equations. How is iodobenzene prepared from it?
questions.answer: Sandmeyer reaction: benzenediazonium chloride is warmed with Cu$_2$Cl$_2$/HCl (or Cu$_2$Br$_2$/HBr) to give chlorobenzene (or bromobenzene) with evolution of N$_2$. C$_6$H$_5$N$_2$$^+$Cl$^-$ + CuCl/HCl → C$_6$H$_5$Cl + N$_2$. Gattermann reaction: the chloro or bromo compound is obtained with copper powder and HCl/HBr: C$_6$H$_5$N$_2$$^+$Cl$^-$ + Cu/HCl → C$_6$H$_5$Cl + N$_2$ + CuCl. Iodobenzene: the diazonium salt is treated with potassium iodide; no copper is needed. C$_6$H$_5$N$_2$$^+$Cl$^-$ + KI → C$_6$H$_5$I + KCl + N$_2$.

questions.q: What is coupling reaction? Explain with the formation of an azo dye (p-hydroxyazobenzene and p-aminoazobenzene).
questions.answer: Benzenediazonium salt reacts with electron-rich aromatic compounds like phenol and aniline at the para position to form brightly coloured azo compounds. This is called coupling reaction; the diazonium cation acts as the electrophile. With phenol in a weakly alkaline medium (pH 9-10): C$_6$H$_5$N$_2$$^+$Cl$^-$ + C$_6$H$_5$OH → p-hydroxyazobenzene (orange dye) + HCl. With aniline in a weakly acidic medium (pH 4-5): gives p-aminoazobenzene (yellow dye). Both contain the -N=N- azo group which connects two aromatic rings; the extended conjugation gives colour.

questions.q: How will you convert (i) nitrobenzene to aniline (ii) aniline to phenol (iii) aniline to benzene? Write only the reagents with equations. Also distinguish between methylamine and aniline.
questions.answer: (i) Nitrobenzene is reduced with Sn/HCl (or Fe/HCl or H$_2$/Pd): C$_6$H$_5$NO$_2$ + 6[H] → C$_6$H$_5$NH$_2$ + 2H$_2$O. (ii) Aniline + NaNO$_2$/HCl at 273-278 K → benzenediazonium chloride; warming with water → phenol + N$_2$. (iii) Benzenediazonium chloride + H$_3$PO$_2$ (hypophosphorous acid) and water → benzene + N$_2$ + H$_3$PO$_3$. Distinction: aniline gives a diazonium salt with NaNO$_2$/HCl at 273 K which couples with beta-naphthol to give an orange-red azo dye (dye test); methylamine on the same treatment gives only nitrogen gas and methanol.

questions.q: Explain with equations any five methods of preparation of amines.
questions.answer: (1) Reduction of nitro compounds: RNO$_2$ + 6[H] (H$_2$/Pd or Sn/HCl) → RNH$_2$ + 2H$_2$O. (2) Ammonolysis of alkyl halides: R-X + NH$_3$ → RNH$_2$ (then secondary, tertiary amines and quaternary salt form; primary is major with excess NH$_3$). (3) Reduction of nitriles with LiAlH$_4$ or H$_2$/Ni: R-CN → RCH$_2$NH$_2$. (4) Reduction of amides with LiAlH$_4$: RCONH$_2$ → RCH$_2$NH$_2$. (5) Gabriel phthalimide synthesis: gives pure primary aliphatic amines. (6) Hoffmann bromamide degradation: RCONH$_2$ + Br$_2$ + 4NaOH → RNH$_2$ + Na$_2$CO$_3$ + 2NaBr + 2H$_2$O (amine has one carbon less).

questions.q: Explain the following reactions of amines with equations: (i) alkylation (ii) acylation (iii) reaction with nitrous acid for primary aliphatic and aromatic amines (iv) carbylamine reaction (v) bromination of aniline.
questions.answer: (i) Alkylation: R-NH$_2$ + R-X → R$_2$NH → R$_3$N → R$_4$N$^+$X$^-$ (quaternary salt). (ii) Acylation: amines react with acid chlorides or anhydrides in the presence of pyridine to form amides: CH$_3$NH$_2$ + CH$_3$COCl → CH$_3$NHCOCH$_3$ + HCl; aniline gives acetanilide. (iii) Nitrous acid (NaNO$_2$ + HCl): aliphatic primary amines give alcohol with N$_2$ evolution (R-NH$_2$ → R-OH + N$_2$); aromatic amines give diazonium salt at 273-278 K: C$_6$H$_5$NH$_2$ → C$_6$H$_5$N$_2$$^+$Cl$^-$. (iv) Carbylamine reaction with CHCl$_3$/alc. KOH gives foul-smelling isocyanide. (v) Bromine water with aniline gives white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromoaniline; to get mono-bromo product, the NH$_2$ is first protected by acetylation.

questions.q: Write any five reactions of benzenediazonium chloride in which the diazo group is replaced, and mention two importance of diazonium salts.
questions.answer: Replacement by: (1) Cl or Br: Cu$_2$Cl$_2$/HCl or Cu$_2$Br$_2$/HBr (Sandmeyer) gives C$_6$H$_5$Cl or C$_6$H$_5$Br. (2) I: KI gives iodobenzene. (3) F: HBF$_4$ forms benzenediazonium fluoroborate, which on heating gives fluorobenzene + BF$_3$ + N$_2$ (Balz-Schiemann). (4) CN: Cu$_2$(CN)$_2$/KCN gives benzonitrile. (5) OH: warming with water gives phenol. (6) H: H$_3$PO$_2$ or ethanol gives benzene. Importance: diazonium salts are intermediates for introducing F, Cl, Br, I, CN, OH groups into the benzene ring, which cannot be done by direct substitution, and for the preparation of azo dyes by coupling.
